variants: We piloted a cloud-based project management tool last year, but adoption was inconsistent across teams and we ultimately reverted to spreadsheets and email for most project tracking. The experience highlighted that tool adoption requires more structured change management than we initially planned for.

A junior engineer built an internal dashboard to visualize our order backlog, which the operations team found useful. However, this was an informal side project with no official support or maintenance plan. When that engineer left, the dashboard became unreliable and was eventually abandoned. We learned that good ideas need institutional backing to survive.

We experimented with a customer self-service portal two years ago after seeing competitors offer similar functionality. We built an MVP with an external agency in 3 months, but customer adoption was disappointing — only 8% of customers created accounts. We did not invest enough in understanding whether our specific customer base actually wanted self-service before building.

We attempted to introduce a weekly innovation brainstorming session across departments, but attendance dropped rapidly after the first month. Participants felt the sessions generated interesting ideas but had no clear path to execution or budget. The initiative faded without producing any tangible outcome.
